title: How Farming Spread Across Neolithic Europe
text:
Consider a question that has occupied prehistorians for over a century: when farming reached Europe, did people move, or did ideas move? The archaeological record shows domesticated wheat, barley, sheep and goats appearing first in south-west Asia and then, over several thousand years, spreading north and west across the continent. The pattern is gradual and fairly regular, which early researchers read as a slow wave of farming families advancing a few kilometres in each generation, absorbing or displacing the hunter-gatherers they met.

Others argued the opposite. Nothing needs to migrate except knowledge: local foragers, seeing the advantages of cultivation, could simply adopt the new crops and animals themselves. Pottery styles and burial customs were used to support both readings, and for decades the debate could not be settled from artefacts alone. What changed the picture was the recovery of ancient DNA from Neolithic skeletons. It shows substantial movement of people from the south-east, but also interbreeding with existing populations, and regions where local communities clearly took up farming on their own terms. The answer is both, and the more interesting question now is why the balance differed so much from place to place.
points: Domesticated crops and animals appear first in south-west Asia and spread across Europe over thousands of years.
One explanation is that farming families themselves migrated slowly, generation by generation.
The rival explanation is that local hunter-gatherers adopted the crops and animals without anyone migrating.
Artefacts such as pottery and burial customs could be read as supporting either view.
Ancient DNA from Neolithic skeletons showed both movement of people and mixing with local populations.
The current answer is that both processes happened, and the question is why the balance varied by region.
